title: Just how bad is this sell-off going to get?
description: Erin Gibbs, Gibbs Wealth Management, and Savita Subramanian, Bank of America Merrill Lynch, discuss what was behind today's 10 percent drop in the Dow.  Stocks plummeted once again on Thursday after President Donald Trump and the Federal Reserve both failed to quell concerns over the economic slowdown stemming from the coronavirus, leading to a historic drop for the U.S. markets.  The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed 2,352.60 points lower, or 9.99%, at 21,200.62. The index had its worst drop since the 1987 “Black Monday” market crash, when it collapsed by more than 22%.The S&P 500 plummeted 9.5% to 2,480.64, joining the Dow in a bear market. The S&P 500 also had its worst day since 1987. The Nasdaq Composite closed 9.4% lower at 7,201.80.  “The coronavirus is scary and people don't know what to expect,” said Kathy Entwistle, senior vice president of wealth management at UBS. “It's like the tsunami is coming. We know it's going to hit any day and nobody knows what the outcome is going to be.”  The major averages got a brief respite during the trading day after the Fed announced it will ramp up its overnight funding operations to more than $500 billion on Thursday. It will then offer more repo operations totaling $1 trillion on Friday. The Fed also expanded the types of securities it would purchase with reserves.   However, stocks quickly traded back towards their session lows as investors awaited more aggressive measures to support the economy and target the virus outbreak directly.  “These changes are being made to address highly unusual disruptions in Treasury financing markets associated with the coronavirus outbreak,” said the statement from the New York Federal Reserve, which conducts these operations on behalf of the Fed. asr.full_text: Savita, how bad is this going to get? I mean, I think it gets worse before it gets better. But I do think that right now it's time to pick stocks. Because what we saw over the last few weeks was an historically indiscriminate sell-off. And what I mean is that stocks didn't behave like stocks. They all fell together. The correlations of stocks in this downturn was higher than we've seen in the past post-crisis downturns. So I think that where we are today is a point at which there are going to be companies that you want to add exposure to right now. And I think that's the best way to deal with this type of market. I think the other critical point that we want to remind investors is that the best market days typically follow the worst market days. So there's a strong impulse to sort of sell everything and hide out in cash after days like today. But I think that that's dangerous. And I think, you know, just to remind you, if you had missed the 10 best days of the past decade,. You would have only made half of the returns that we actually enjoyed since 2010. You would have made 95% gains instead of 190% gains. So I think that this is the time to stay disciplined, you know, maybe have a quality and a defensive bias,. And also pick stocks because, again, by our math,. This was the most indiscriminate selling of stocks that we've seen. Okay, Erin, so Savita says time to pick stocks. Is she right? I think we could still have some more room. I think we might have another month of sort of these negative shocks. Certainly we might stabilize tomorrow,. But I think particularly as a lot of the restrictions hit,. It's going to be more of a psychological factor. Where people are suddenly having really significant changes. And how they behave and what they can do. And if we're anything like Italy,. The initial bans on large group gatherings,. About three to four weeks, you get complete lockdowns. And so I think that might be really the catalyst. For particularly in Wall Street today,. We had a large group ban go into effect. I think that certainly is going to be on the minds. Of a lot of institutional investors. And so we could certainly go down. And test the 2018 lows of about 2250. That also just brings us down to about 14 times forward earnings, which still isn't extraordinarily cheap when you look at it historically. It's definitely cheap, but not extreme low. So I think there's room. However, again, I think people need to start thinking about what stocks are going to benefit from this new behavior and changes in behavior and look at the companies that can potentially come out of this ahead and leading the rebound. Thank you.
